 TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

          Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (“Oncor”) and LCRA Transmission Services

Corporation (“LCRA TSC” and together with Oncor, the “Applicants”) respectfully file this reply

brief on Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 11 and 13 (“Reply”) related to the transmission projects

hereinafter called the “Import Path 2 Projects,” comprised of the Bell County East Switch to Big

Hill Substation 765 kV transmission line project and the Big Hill Substation to Sand Lake Switch

765 kV transmission line project. SOAH Order No. 35 sets a deadline of October 19, 2026, to file

reply briefs. 1 Therefore, this Reply is timely filed.

    I.    INTRODUCTION

          On October 7, 2026, Applicants filed their Brief on Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 11 and

13. 2 Twenty other briefs were filed by various intervenors and Commission Staff (“Staff”) on the

same day.        In their briefs, intervenors repeat arguments that have been raised and refuted

countlessly throughout this proceeding. Those arguments center on the weight given to the Electric

Reliability Council of Texas, Inc.’s (“ERCOT”) recommendations, the time by which the Import

Path 2 Projects are needed, the credibility of ERCOT’s load forecasts, and the sufficiency of the

studies on which Applicants rely to establish need, among other issues. Each of these arguments

fails.

          Unlike the intervenors challenging the need for the Import Path 2 Projects, Staff agrees

with Applicants on both remanded issues. Staff concludes that the Import Path 2 Projects, in

conjunction with the other Permian Basin Reliability Plan Study (“Permian Basin Reliability

Plan”) projects, will resolve reliability criteria violations under North American Electric

     II.    PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUE NO. 11


Are the proposed transmission facilities necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards?


           A. Requiring studies that isolate Import Path 2 has no foundation in the law and is
              inconsistent with Commission precedent.

           Among the briefs filed by intervenors related to Preliminary Order Issue No. 11, a common

argument is that Applicants should have, but did not, provide a study that removed the Import Path

2 Projects and reflected a violation of state or federal reliability standards caused by that removal. 5

But neither PURA § 37.056 nor 16 TAC § 25.101 requires a “partial build” or “removal case”

study. Those provisions direct the Commission to consider enumerated factors, including the

adequacy of existing service and the need for additional service, and they provide that the

Commission will give great weight to ERCOT’s recommendation that a project is needed for

reliability. A partial build analysis is not among the enumerated factors, and the Commission

approved the Permian Basin Reliability Plan as well as Import Paths 1 and 3 without one. 6

           The Commission’s own decisions foreclose the isolation requirement.                          In its Order

Approving the Reliability Plan for the Permian Basin Region, the Commission approved the

Permian Basin Reliability Plan and authorized the applicable transmission service providers

(“TSPs”) to begin preparing certificate of convenience and necessity (“CCN”) applications for all

three 765 kV import paths identified in Table 7.5 of the Permian Basin Reliability Plan. 7 On April

           B. Intervenors’ arguments that Applicants must prove there is sufficient generation

           Several intervenors argue that Applicants failed to prove that sufficient generation is

available at the Bell County East endpoint to transmit power westward, and that Central Texas will

need its own imports. 19 These arguments treat the Import Path 2 Projects as a radial line, and more

than that, a radial line that somehow can carry only the output of generators physically located in

Bell County. Respectfully, such arguments fundamentally misunderstand the operation of the

interconnected ERCOT grid and the manner in which the 765 kV projects are designed to function.

All three stations connected to the Import Path 2 Projects are currently connected to the existing

ERCOT 345 kV transmission system, which serves the entire state, and the Import Path 2 Projects,

in conjunction with the other Permian Basin Reliability Plan upgrades, will improve the reliability,

strength, and stability of the overall transmission system. 20 Power flowing over the Import Path 2

Projects will be drawn from generation across the entire interconnected ERCOT transmission grid,

not from a single substation or county.

            ERCOT designed the import paths with consideration for the reliability of the entire

capability in West Texas while also reducing curtailment of cost-effective renewable generation

hub ignores the fundamental bi-directional basis of transmission system design.

system that addresses Central Texas and Far West Texas needs together and is sequencing them

as appropriate to meet all applicable reliability standards; the existence of Central Texas import

needs does not mean that the Import Path 2 Projects cannot perform their reliability function. As

Staff explained in its Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision, ERCOT’s planning models,

including the other components of the 765 kV Strategic Transmission Expansion Plan (“STEP”),

           D. The fact that alternative import paths at other voltage levels would also meet state
              or federal reliability standards is not proof that the Import Path 2 Projects are

           Multiple parties submitted briefs citing the Permian Basin Reliability Plan to argue that the

765 kV import path upgrades are not necessary to meet state and federal reliability standards. For

intervenors such as Mr. Aaron Howton, the Mewhinney Family, and the Cherokee Creek Aligned

Intervenors, this argument rests on the fact that the Permian Basin Reliability Plan identified three

potential import path voltage options to address the identified reliability need: 765 kV; 500 kV;

and 345 kV. This argument, however, proves the reliability need for the Import Path 2 Projects

under federal and state reliability standards.                Every alternative ERCOT identified required

substantial new import-path capacity into the Permian Basin because the existing system violates

TPL-001-5.1 and ERCOT criteria without it. ERCOT concluded that “multiple import paths would

be needed to transfer power to the Permian Basin region across the ERCOT system to reliably

serve the projected load.” 36 The 345 kV, 500 kV, and 765 kV options were mutually exclusive

ways to deliver that required import capability. None of those voltage plans was a no-build option.

Including a no-build component to any of the options would result in a plan that would not address
